title: Ideas You Cannot See
tagline: Seven women in a hall, each carrying a symbol. How medieval teachers kept justice, courage and logic in mind, and how you can too.
card: How to turn abstract words and ideas into people, symbols and scenes, with the old advice of Aquinas and the old habit of personification.
goal: you will learn four ways to make an abstract idea visible (a symbol, a person, a scene, an emotion), and use them to keep a list of abstract words.

left_off.q: What is a hub in a palace network?
left_off.a: The central place that connects the other palaces.
A vivid link from the last place of one palace to the first place of the next.

left_off.q: Why should each palace be distinct?
left_off.a: So the rooms of one subject do not get mixed with those of another.

text: Imagine a long hall in a medieval university. Seven women stand between the columns, each holding something. One has a book, one a pair of scales, one a pair of compasses, one a counting frame, one a lute, one a globe. They are not real women. They are the seven liberal arts, the subjects every student had to study: grammar, rhetoric, logic, arithmetic, geometry, music and astronomy.
Artists painted them again and again. They did it because an idea with no face is hard to hold, and an idea with a face, a costume and something to carry is easy.

check.a: Personifications of the seven liberal arts, each carrying a symbol.

parts.talk: If you had to paint 'justice' as a person, what would she wear and carry?

text: The great thirteenth-century thinker Thomas Aquinas wrote about memory, following the old Roman handbooks. He gave advice that sounds modern. Put the things you want to remember in an order. Attach them to striking images, because plain ones slip away. Give them your close attention. And go over them often.

He also noticed the difficulty this lesson is about: the ideas that matter most, such as truth, duty or fairness, are the ones with no picture. His answer was the old one. Use likenesses: a picture that stands for the idea, even if it is not the idea.

check.q: What were Aquinas's four pieces of advice?
check.a: Put things in order, attach striking images, give close attention, and go over them often.

parts.talk: Which of those four do you find hardest to do?

text: Later, in the sixteenth century, the philosopher Giordano Bruno designed enormous systems of images for abstract ideas, with wheels of figures that stood for qualities and concepts. They were too complicated to be useful for most people. But the principle was right: an abstract idea needs a body.
You will not need a wheel. You need four small tools, and a habit of asking, whenever you meet an idea, what could I see that stands for this?

check.q: What is the principle behind all of these systems?
check.a: An abstract idea needs a body: a picture, person or symbol that stands for it.

parts.talk: Think of an abstract word you find hard. What could stand for it?

image.alt: An engraving of seven women in a columned hall, each holding a symbol such as a book, scales, compasses, a counting frame, a lute and a globe.

words.m: an idea you cannot see or touch. Justice is abstract.
something you can see or touch. A pair of scales is concrete.
showing an idea as a person.
a thing that stands for an idea. A dove is a symbol of peace.
something that looks or acts like something else.
a good or bad feature of a person or thing. Courage is a quality.

source: Aquinas's four pieces of advice follow the Roman handbook tradition. Bruno's memory systems date from the 1580s. Told here in our own words.
method_heading: Four ways to give an idea a body

method.x: To remember an abstract idea, make it concrete: turn it into something you can see, hear and feel.

head: Tool
How
Example
rows: Use an object that traditionally stands for it
Justice: scales. Peace: a dove. Time: an hourglass.
Make the idea a person doing something, or use a person famous for it
Courage: a firefighter in the flames. Wisdom: an old owl-eyed woman.
Inflation: prices on a shop sign rise like a balloon and float away.
Put in the emotion the idea brings
Freedom: running barefoot down a hill with the wind in your hair.

items.x: Symbol, person, scene or feeling. A mix is best.
On a peg, in a palace place, or in a chain.

items.h: Check that it brings the idea back.
items.x: Look at the picture, then say what it means. If it does not work, change it.

method.title: Democracy
method.given: Democracy: a system where the people choose their government by voting.
lines: People vote and the majority decides.
A crowd of thousands queues up, each person dropping a paper hat into a huge box. The box decides who wears the crown.
The cheer when the result is read out.
method.pic: A great crowd drops paper hats into a giant box, and the box chooses who wears the crown.

method.x: Small grammatical words, such as although or because, have no pictures either. Give each a fixed picture from its sound, as in the keyword method (lesson 16): because as a buzzing bee holding a banner that says CAUSE; although as a giant letter A made of dough.

ask: what could I see
that stands for this?
Take the word justice and describe aloud a symbol, a person, a scene and a feeling for it.

try.title: Symbol or scene?
try.prompt: Match each abstract idea to a good symbol.

try.title: Freedom
try.prompt: Make a scene for freedom. Use at least two of the four tools and one sense.
try.model: A runner kicks off her shoes and races barefoot down a green hill. A broken chain is flying behind her like a kite, and the wind roars in her ears.
checks: It uses at least two tools.

try.title: Inflation
try.prompt: Make a scene for inflation (prices rising). Use a scene and a feeling.
try.model: A shopkeeper changes the price of a loaf from 1 to 2 to 4 to 8, and the loaf swells like a balloon and floats off. The queue groans.
checks: It would remind me of the word.

try.title: Courage and evidence
try.prompt: Make one scene for courage and one for evidence. Use a person for one and a symbol for the other.
try.model: Courage: a small child in a cape walks calmly past a giant dragon. Evidence: a detective's magnifying glass finds a footprint, which sits in a glass case under a spotlight.
checks: One uses a person, one a symbol.

try.q: Which is the best picture for 'patience'?
opts: A gardener waiting calmly beside a seed that is just beginning to open
The word PATIENCE in large letters
try.why: A person doing something that shows the idea, with a symbol (the seed).

try.title: Explain your pictures
try.prompt: Say the word, the picture and why the picture stands for the idea, for freedom, inflation and courage.

cards: An object that stands for the idea: scales for justice.
The idea as a person, or a famous person for it.
The idea happening: prices rising, a crowd voting.
Order; striking images; close attention; go over them often.
Look at the picture and say what it means; if it fails, change it.

opts: Something you can see or touch

quiz.q: Which is a symbol for justice?

opts: Showing an idea as a person
quiz.why: Giving an idea a human form.

quiz.q: What should you do if a picture does not bring back the idea?
quiz.why: A picture must point to the idea.

challenge.title: Memory challenge: six abstract words
challenge.intro: Learn six ideas in order, each with a picture: justice, freedom, democracy, inflation, courage, evidence. Type them back in order.
challenge.study: Scales; a barefoot runner; a box of paper hats; a floating loaf; a child past a dragon; a footprint under a spotlight.

look_back.q: Why use more than one palace?
look_back.a: One palace holds only as many items as it has places.

look_back.q: What does a three-digit syllable consist of?
look_back.a: A consonant, a vowel and a consonant.
Find a sound-alike and join it to the meaning in a picture.
Replacing a word you cannot picture with something that sounds like it or stands for it.

can_do: name four ways to make an idea concrete.
turn an abstract word into a picture and test it.
keep a list of abstract words in order.
reflect: Which abstract words in your own subject keep slipping away? What would their pictures be?
